match.reason: The closest bank cards cover first and third person narrators and reliability in general, but neither teaches omniscient versus limited narration or narrative distance as the central idea, so a new point fits better.

draft.title: Omniscient and limited narration
card: The narrator knows what every character thinks and feels, and can move between their minds. The narrator may also know things that no character knows.
The narrator stays close to one character and shows only what that character sees, thinks and feels. Other characters are known only from the outside.
Both are usually told in the third person, with he, she or they. Limited narration can also be told by a character as I, but this point is about the third person.
This is how near the telling sits to a character's mind. A close distance gives a reader a character's feelings. A far distance gives a view from outside, like a camera.
draft.remember: Omniscient narrators can enter many minds. Limited narrators stay with one. Distance is how close the telling is to a mind.

a.q: Which narrator can tell the reader what several different characters are thinking?
opts: An omniscient narrator
A limited narrator
A narrator at a far distance
A narrator who stays with one character
a.why: An omniscient narrator knows every character's thoughts and can move between their minds. A limited narrator is tempting, but it stays close to one character and shows the others only from outside.
a.clue: Think about which narrator can enter every mind.

b.q: In a story, the narrator says: Leila wondered if the interview had gone badly. Her interviewer, Mr Ortiz, was already thinking about lunch. What kind of narration is this?
opts: Omniscient, because it gives two characters' thoughts
Limited, because it names only one character
Omniscient, because it uses the third person
Limited, because it describes Leila's feelings
b.why: The narrator reports both Leila's thoughts and Mr Ortiz's thoughts, so it moves between minds. That is omniscient. Limited narration would stay with Leila and show Mr Ortiz only from outside. The third person alone does not make narration omniscient.
b.clue: Count whose thoughts the narrator reveals.

b.best: Omniscient, because it gives two characters' thoughts
